note: Original independent MAIC exam draft, not active or approved; question-level reviewer signoff, approved source PDF and live testing required.

questions.stem: What distinguishes scheduled broadcast from on-demand distribution?
options: Assume all media is fiction
Broadcast follows a planned program time while on-demand access is selected by users
Use public-domain status for all web content
Issue completion certificates from self-tests
questions.rationale: The manual compares different audience access models. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: What is the principal question media studies asks about a program's creation?
options: Treat every social view as verified evidence
Ignore who funds or distributes media
Assume all media is fiction
Who produces, finances, distributes and can access the content
questions.rationale: Production and ownership affect media interpretation. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: What should learners distinguish when interpreting media?
options: Use public-domain status for all web content
Issue completion certificates from self-tests
Fiction, assertions, opinions and verified factual claims
Treat every social view as verified evidence
questions.rationale: Genre influences what the content is claiming. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: Which activity is part of responsible media program planning?
options: Identifying target viewers, rights and accessibility needs
Ignore who funds or distributes media
Assume all media is fiction
Use public-domain status for all web content
questions.rationale: Audience needs and usage permissions belong in the plan. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: What is a possible distribution path for one documentary?
options: Issue completion certificates from self-tests
Treat every social view as verified evidence
A scheduled television airing followed by an online replay
Ignore who funds or distributes media
questions.rationale: Programs may be delivered through more than one platform. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: What principle applies when an entertainment program makes factual claims?
options: Those claims still require proportionate verification
Assume all media is fiction
Use public-domain status for all web content
Issue completion certificates from self-tests
questions.rationale: Entertainment framing does not remove factual responsibility. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: What does the self-practice rubric in the manual represent?
options: Treat every social view as verified evidence
A learning aid rather than an official academic grade
Ignore who funds or distributes media
Assume all media is fiction
questions.rationale: Self-review is not equivalent to formal certification. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: Why should an original classroom scenario be labeled fictional?
options: Use public-domain status for all web content
Issue completion certificates from self-tests
So learners do not mistake invented cases for actual media events
Treat every social view as verified evidence
questions.rationale: Fictional examples must not impersonate real evidence. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: A documentary is broadcast at 8 p.m. and offered later in a catalog. What changes for a viewer?
options: The factual claims become exempt from checking
The choice between scheduled viewing and on-demand selection
Rights automatically expand worldwide
The program becomes a different genre
questions.rationale: Viewing access changes but content obligations remain. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: An invented classroom program depicts fictional people. What is its accurate designation?
options: A verified broadcast documentary
An authenticated eyewitness program
A fictional teaching scenario
An official government communication
questions.rationale: The program must not claim to record real people and events. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 2.

questions.stem: What is a broadcast schedule?
options: Assume streaming is only live news
Ignore timing and audience choices
Assume every type of media requires images
An arrangement of programs for planned transmission times
questions.rationale: Scheduled transmission differs from user-selected playback. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: What is an on-demand media library?
options: Treat staged scenes as documentary witnesses
Use inaccurate program descriptions
Assume streaming is only live news
A catalog whose programs viewers select when available
questions.rationale: On-demand access permits viewer choice. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: What type of medium emphasizes sound without required images?
options: Ignore timing and audience choices
Assume every type of media requires images
Radio or an audio-only program
Treat staged scenes as documentary witnesses
questions.rationale: Audio-first formats differ from television. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: Why can reality-style programs create factual confusion?
options: Use inaccurate program descriptions
Staged and actual events can appear similar without clear labeling
Assume streaming is only live news
Ignore timing and audience choices
questions.rationale: Genres mixing reality and production require transparency. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: What is an interstitial segment in broadcast planning?
options: A short item placed between longer programs
Assume every type of media requires images
Treat staged scenes as documentary witnesses
Use inaccurate program descriptions
questions.rationale: Short continuity segments may fill and bridge schedules. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: What should an online program listing contain?
options: Assume streaming is only live news
Ignore timing and audience choices
Assume every type of media requires images
An accurate synopsis, language information and accessibility details
questions.rationale: Metadata helps discovery and informs viewers. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: Why is streaming not a genre in itself?
options: The delivery method can carry many kinds of content
Treat staged scenes as documentary witnesses
Use inaccurate program descriptions
Assume streaming is only live news
questions.rationale: Streaming refers to distribution rather than content category. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: What is a common concern when adapting TV content into short social clips?
options: Ignore timing and audience choices
Assume every type of media requires images
Treat staged scenes as documentary witnesses
The shorter version may omit necessary factual context
questions.rationale: All formats must preserve core meaning. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: A 24-minute program is placed within a 30-minute slot. How much time remains for other elements?
options: 6 minutes
4 minutes
24 minutes
54 minutes
questions.rationale: Thirty minus twenty-four equals six minutes. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: A radio producer wants listeners to understand a chart shown in the video version. What is necessary?
options: Rely solely on chart colors
Remove the explanation from the radio version
Describe the essential information audibly
Assume radio audiences have a screen
questions.rationale: Audio-first programs must communicate essential facts through sound. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 3.

questions.stem: What makes a commissioning proposal more than a title?
options: Approve production without a budget
A brief with purpose, target viewers, format, costs, rights and plan
Ignore archive clearance and contingency
Leave all factual review unassigned
questions.rationale: Production feasibility requires more than a concept name. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: Which role normally coordinates program scope and delivery?
options: The producer
Treat a program title as a complete brief
Exclude final technical checks from the schedule
Approve production without a budget
questions.rationale: Producing involves coordination across teams. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: Which role should check the evidence behind a factual report?
options: Ignore archive clearance and contingency
Leave all factual review unassigned
Treat a program title as a complete brief
A researcher or responsible editorial verifier
questions.rationale: Factual claims require assigned verification. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: Why include accessibility in the production budget?
options: Exclude final technical checks from the schedule
Approve production without a budget
Captions and related services may require resources
Ignore archive clearance and contingency
questions.rationale: Accessibility is an intended deliverable. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: What should a production schedule include after filming?
options: Leave all factual review unassigned
Editing, clearance, quality assurance and final delivery
Treat a program title as a complete brief
Exclude final technical checks from the schedule
questions.rationale: Shooting is one stage in a longer workflow. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: Why are archive materials a rights and cost issue?
options: Permission may be needed for particular uses or territories
Approve production without a budget
Ignore archive clearance and contingency
Leave all factual review unassigned
questions.rationale: Access does not guarantee unrestricted distribution. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: What is the risk of committing to a large series without confirmed resources?
options: Treat a program title as a complete brief
Exclude final technical checks from the schedule
Approve production without a budget
The promised scope may not be feasible
questions.rationale: Budgets should include realistic capacities and contingencies. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: Why explicitly name review responsibilities in small teams?
options: Ignore archive clearance and contingency
Leave all factual review unassigned
Treat a program title as a complete brief
Combining roles can leave quality checks without a clear owner
questions.rationale: Accountability prevents important omissions. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: A 30-minute program also needs archive music costing $250 and caption work costing $150. What is their combined budget?
questions.rationale: Two known production costs add to $400. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: A team has one editor acting as caption checker as well. What remains necessary?
options: Assume combined roles eliminate the checks
Skip all final QA because staff is small
Explicitly schedule both editing and caption review
Ignore proofing captions
questions.rationale: Combining roles does not remove responsibility. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 4.

questions.stem: Why does a broadcast grid need precise duration planning?
options: Assume live events always end on time
Give no warning about changed program times
Programs and scheduled elements must fit their transmission slots
Ignore suitability for younger viewers
questions.rationale: Timing is a core part of scheduling. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: What may disrupt a planned lineup?
options: Set every commercial break by one global rule
Treat clickbait thumbnails as accurate metadata
A live event that runs later than expected
Assume live events always end on time
questions.rationale: Live timing uncertainty affects subsequent programs. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: What should a continuity announcement convey after a schedule change?
options: Give no warning about changed program times
Accurate updated information about the lineup
Ignore suitability for younger viewers
Set every commercial break by one global rule
questions.rationale: Current information helps audience expectations. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: How should a scheduler treat commercial-break rules?
options: Treat clickbait thumbnails as accurate metadata
Assume live events always end on time
Check requirements for the actual jurisdiction and broadcaster
Give no warning about changed program times
questions.rationale: There is no single globally applicable commercial-break rule. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: What changes when a program becomes on-demand?
options: Ignore suitability for younger viewers
Set every commercial break by one global rule
Discovery and catalog metadata replace fixed viewing-time dependence
Treat clickbait thumbnails as accurate metadata
questions.rationale: On-demand audiences choose playback times. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: Why is a misleading thumbnail undesirable?
options: It can create false expectations even when it attracts clicks
Assume live events always end on time
Give no warning about changed program times
Ignore suitability for younger viewers
questions.rationale: Metadata should match program content. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: Which factor matters for children-oriented programming?
options: Set every commercial break by one global rule
Age suitability and relevant content safeguards
Treat clickbait thumbnails as accurate metadata
Assume live events always end on time
questions.rationale: Appropriate programming must consider its target audience. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: Why keep recovery options for live broadcasts?
options: Give no warning about changed program times
Ignore suitability for younger viewers
Set every commercial break by one global rule
Unexpected overruns may require changes to the following schedule
questions.rationale: Operational planning should consider timing disruptions. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: A 60-minute lineup has 22, 18 and 14 minutes of content. How much remains?
options: 4 minutes
6 minutes
8 minutes
54 minutes
questions.rationale: 22+18+14=54 minutes leaving six. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: A live event overruns a planned 20-minute segment by four minutes. What is the relevant first response?
options: Update the rundown and communicate resulting schedule changes
Invent an earlier ending time
Assume no program will be affected
Describe the event as recorded rather than live
questions.rationale: Timing overruns may disrupt following content. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 5.

questions.stem: Why is a streaming play not automatically one distinct viewer?
options: Treat a play count as unique persons
Use audience ratings as proof of accuracy
Treat public comments as a random population survey
One person may generate multiple recorded plays
questions.rationale: Metrics count different units. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: What is an audience measurement denominator?
options: The defined total population or events used in a rate
Assume two platforms use identical metrics
Ignore groups excluded from measurement
Treat a play count as unique persons
questions.rationale: Meaningful rate comparisons require a common basis. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: Why not directly equate a TV rating with a web view count?
options: Use audience ratings as proof of accuracy
Treat public comments as a random population survey
The sampling populations and definitions may be different
Assume two platforms use identical metrics
questions.rationale: Different metrics are not directly comparable. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: What can a completion rate tell a producer?
options: The share of eligible starts reaching a defined endpoint
Ignore groups excluded from measurement
Treat a play count as unique persons
Use audience ratings as proof of accuracy
questions.rationale: Completion describes measured behavior, not accuracy. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: What is one limitation of online audience comments?
options: Treat public comments as a random population survey
Assume two platforms use identical metrics
Ignore groups excluded from measurement
Participation may reflect self-selection rather than everyone
questions.rationale: Feedback may not represent the entire audience. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: What can hidden audience segments reveal?
options: Treat a play count as unique persons
Use audience ratings as proof of accuracy
Treat public comments as a random population survey
The program serves some language or region groups poorly
questions.rationale: Aggregates can conceal accessibility gaps. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: Why might a small community program still matter?
options: Assume two platforms use identical metrics
It may provide high public value to a specific audience
Ignore groups excluded from measurement
Treat a play count as unique persons
questions.rationale: Broad popularity and social value differ. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: What else should accompany reach metrics in a quality review?
options: Use audience ratings as proof of accuracy
Correction, comprehension and accessibility outcomes
Treat public comments as a random population survey
Assume two platforms use identical metrics
questions.rationale: Audience volume alone does not measure responsible performance. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: A stream logs 360 completions from 600 compatible starts. What is the completion rate?
questions.rationale: 360 divided by 600 equals 0.60. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: A platform records 800 plays from 500 identified users. What is justified?
options: Recorded plays exceed the number of identified users
Exactly 800 distinct people watched
Every user watched exactly once
No user replayed any content
questions.rationale: Plays and unique users measure different events. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 6.

questions.stem: What does media representation analysis examine?
options: Claim music proves a person's guilt
Who is portrayed, omitted and framed in the content
Use archival scenes as current without disclosure
Assign invented statements to real interview subjects
questions.rationale: Editing and casting shape visible perspectives. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: How can a genuine quote become misleading?
options: Move quotes between questions without checking context
Editing it as an answer to a different question
Treat repetition as independent corroboration
Claim music proves a person's guilt
questions.rationale: Context is part of quote accuracy. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: What is media literacy intended to improve?
options: Critical evaluation of content sources, purposes and evidence
Use archival scenes as current without disclosure
Assign invented statements to real interview subjects
Move quotes between questions without checking context
questions.rationale: Literacy considers origin, meaning and credibility. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: What does a dramatic soundtrack establish about a person's guilt?
options: Treat repetition as independent corroboration
Nothing without independent relevant evidence
Claim music proves a person's guilt
Use archival scenes as current without disclosure
questions.rationale: Emotion is not factual corroboration. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: How should historical footage be used in a factual program?
options: With accurate date and contextual labeling
Assign invented statements to real interview subjects
Move quotes between questions without checking context
Treat repetition as independent corroboration
questions.rationale: Archival scenes must not impersonate current events. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: Why can repeating one report on several channels fail to corroborate it?
options: Claim music proves a person's guilt
Use archival scenes as current without disclosure
The channels may all depend on the same unsupported source
Assign invented statements to real interview subjects
questions.rationale: Independent evidence differs from repetition. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: Does fair representation require every character to be portrayed positively?
options: Move quotes between questions without checking context
Treat repetition as independent corroboration
Claim music proves a person's guilt
No, it requires sound context and avoidance of careless generalization
questions.rationale: Critical representation is not compulsory flattery. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: What should a creator avoid when using a real person's likeness?
options: Use archival scenes as current without disclosure
Assign invented statements to real interview subjects
Attributing invented testimony as if the person actually said it
Move quotes between questions without checking context
questions.rationale: Fabricated personal claims misrepresent identity. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: A program edits a speaker's answer after an unrelated question. What is the core ethical problem?
options: The original words were not grammatically complex
The interview lasted too long
The edited scene has no background music
The edited context may misrepresent what the speaker meant
questions.rationale: Factual meaning depends on context. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: An archival crowd clip is used to illustrate today's event. What protects against a false implication?
options: Present it as recorded today
Use a more dramatic soundtrack
Label the archive date and illustrative context
Remove the original date
questions.rationale: Archive identification prevents misrepresentation. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 7.

questions.stem: What should sponsorship identification communicate?
options: Assume all internet music is free to air
Treat public visibility as unlimited consent
That content is paid or furnished and identify the relevant sponsor as required
Hide the identity of a paying sponsor
questions.rationale: Commercial influence should be transparent. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: Why can an online song still require permission for broadcast use?
options: Public availability is not the same as distribution rights
Apply U.S. broadcast rules to every service worldwide
Use any archive footage without checking its license
Assume all internet music is free to air
questions.rationale: Rights must be cleared for intended uses. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: What does a media clearance register record?
options: Treat public visibility as unlimited consent
Asset owner, permission, allowed uses and relevant restrictions
Hide the identity of a paying sponsor
Apply U.S. broadcast rules to every service worldwide
questions.rationale: Rights documentation supports lawful distribution. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: Why must regulatory guidance identify the jurisdiction?
options: Use any archive footage without checking its license
Assume all internet music is free to air
Different countries and distribution categories apply different rules
Treat public visibility as unlimited consent
questions.rationale: U.S. broadcast rules should not be assumed universal. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: What is a potential limit on a music license?
options: Territory, platform, duration or language version
Hide the identity of a paying sponsor
Apply U.S. broadcast rules to every service worldwide
Use any archive footage without checking its license
questions.rationale: Licenses can be restricted by use. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: What makes a documentary participant's consent relevant to online clips?
options: Assume all internet music is free to air
Treat public visibility as unlimited consent
Permission for one use may not cover unrelated reuse
Hide the identity of a paying sponsor
questions.rationale: Rights and consent can have scope. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: Which media choice poses a privacy risk?
options: Apply U.S. broadcast rules to every service worldwide
Publishing unnecessary personal identifiers from raw footage
Use any archive footage without checking its license
Assume all internet music is free to air
questions.rationale: Accessibility of a file does not erase privacy concerns. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: What should a producer do when rights are unclear?
options: Treat public visibility as unlimited consent
Clarify permissions and seek qualified review if necessary
Hide the identity of a paying sponsor
Apply U.S. broadcast rules to every service worldwide
questions.rationale: Uncertain rights should not be ignored. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: A license permits a song for one domestic TV airing only. Can it be assumed to cover a worldwide replay?
options: No, the permitted use and territory must be checked
Yes, all music licenses cover global streaming
Yes, paying once transfers all rights
Yes, if the song is popular
questions.rationale: License scope may be limited by platform and territory. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: A fictional commercial segment is paid for by a sponsor. What should producers check before transmission?
options: How to conceal the sponsor from viewers
Whether a larger font alone makes the advertisement truthful
Whether compensation eliminates editorial responsibility
Applicable sponsorship disclosure and identification obligations
questions.rationale: Commercial consideration can trigger specific disclosure obligations. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 8.

questions.stem: What is an accessibility benefit of accurate subtitles?
options: Depend entirely on a colored graphic for key facts
Making spoken content available to additional audiences
Ignore differences among language versions
Assume all viewers have unlimited connectivity
questions.rationale: Subtitles communicate speech non-audibly. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: Why can audio-only viewers miss a critical on-screen number?
options: Assume subtitles need no proofreading
The information was not spoken or otherwise made available
Correct only one platform after a serious error
Depend entirely on a colored graphic for key facts
questions.rationale: Audio versions need equivalent essential facts. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: Why may translated graphics need different layouts?
options: Ignore differences among language versions
Assume all viewers have unlimited connectivity
Assume subtitles need no proofreading
Text length and direction can vary by language
questions.rationale: Localization requires visual adaptation. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: What should happen after correcting a factual error across versions?
options: Correct only one platform after a serious error
Depend entirely on a colored graphic for key facts
Check which platforms still carry the old statement
Ignore differences among language versions
questions.rationale: Multichannel corrections need propagation. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: What may prevent some people from streaming a program?
options: Connectivity, device or data costs
Assume all viewers have unlimited connectivity
Assume subtitles need no proofreading
Correct only one platform after a serious error
questions.rationale: Access conditions differ by delivery system. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: Why may a broadcast premiere plus online replay be useful?
options: Depend entirely on a colored graphic for key facts
Ignore differences among language versions
Assume all viewers have unlimited connectivity
The two channels may serve different access needs
questions.rationale: Distribution diversity can improve inclusion. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: Why can captioning be hard to add only at the final moment?
options: Assume subtitles need no proofreading
Timing and visual space should be planned earlier
Correct only one platform after a serious error
Depend entirely on a colored graphic for key facts
questions.rationale: Accessibility is part of production design. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: Why should localized programs retain careful source wording?
options: Ignore differences among language versions
Assume all viewers have unlimited connectivity
Assume subtitles need no proofreading
Translation must not turn uncertainty into an unsupported fact
questions.rationale: A localized version needs the same evidentiary standard. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: An English clip has accurate captions but its translated graphic says a different date. What should happen?
options: Correct the translated date against the verified source
Publish both contradictory dates
Treat translation as exempt from checking
Remove the original source record
questions.rationale: Localized variants must preserve factual accuracy. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: A radio audience cannot see a key phone number shown on TV. Which adaptation is appropriate?
options: Read the number aloud clearly and verify it
Show a brighter graphic in the radio program
Assume radio listeners see television subtitles
Replace the number with unverified contact information
questions.rationale: Equivalent audio information supports access. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 9.

questions.stem: What must final program QA check beyond the render status?
options: Treat successful rendering as full editorial approval
Present a generated actor as a genuine witness
Conceal all corrections from previous viewers
Factual accuracy, sound, captions, rights and playback
questions.rationale: Technical file completion is only one quality aspect. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: What should a content recommendation ranking not be mistaken for?
options: A direct measure of factual truth or public value
Assume recommendation ranking establishes accuracy
Ignore subtitle errors in numerical statements
Treat successful rendering as full editorial approval
questions.rationale: Recommendations support discovery, not verification. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: How may AI-generated characters be used ethically?
options: Present a generated actor as a genuine witness
As clearly labeled synthetic or fictional material when appropriate
Conceal all corrections from previous viewers
Assume recommendation ranking establishes accuracy
questions.rationale: Synthetic production must not impersonate documentary witnesses. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: Why must automated transcripts be reviewed?
options: Ignore subtitle errors in numerical statements
They may misstate names, figures or meaning
Treat successful rendering as full editorial approval
Present a generated actor as a genuine witness
questions.rationale: Tools can introduce factual errors. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: What helps build audience trust when a program contains an error?
options: Conceal all corrections from previous viewers
Assume recommendation ranking establishes accuracy
Ignore subtitle errors in numerical statements
A visible, specific and traceable correction
questions.rationale: Transparent revision supports accountability. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: Why should program descriptions be reviewed for accuracy?
options: Treat successful rendering as full editorial approval
Present a generated actor as a genuine witness
A misleading synopsis can misstate what viewers will see
Conceal all corrections from previous viewers
questions.rationale: Metadata is also a public representation. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: Which objective might matter beyond ratings?
options: Assume recommendation ranking establishes accuracy
Ignore subtitle errors in numerical statements
Audience comprehension or accessibility of important information
Treat successful rendering as full editorial approval
questions.rationale: Quality goals can be broader than popularity. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: How should teams evaluate edited footage before release?
options: Present a generated actor as a genuine witness
Conceal all corrections from previous viewers
Assume recommendation ranking establishes accuracy
Check whether cuts and narration preserve honest context
questions.rationale: Editing should not create false factual implications. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: A rendered program contains a false surname. What does a reliable revision process do?
options: Keep the error because the file rendered
Correct the name and record the updated release
Erase every trace of earlier distribution
Rely on platform rankings to fix the error
questions.rationale: Specific, traceable corrections improve accountability. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: A recommendation algorithm ranks a clip first. What is not established?
options: That the system made a ranking
That the clip appeared in a recommendation view
That someone could encounter the clip
That the clip is factually accurate
questions.rationale: Ranking is not fact verification. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 10.

questions.stem: How long is the fictional cultural pilot's complete planned program?
options: Call broadcast-only music permission worldwide streaming rights
Remove crucial context from an interview silently
30 minutes
Describe staged acts as documentary evidence
questions.rationale: The five segment durations total 30 minutes. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: Which piece of a production plan should identify music distribution restrictions?
options: The rights and clearance matrix
Treat each segment as having unlimited airtime
Guarantee all contracts are already cleared
Call broadcast-only music permission worldwide streaming rights
questions.rationale: Licensing must be considered separately by use. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: What is wrong with silently changing an interview answer to shorten a live program?
options: Remove crucial context from an interview silently
Describe staged acts as documentary evidence
Treat each segment as having unlimited airtime
The edit could alter the speaker's meaning
questions.rationale: Timing pressure does not justify a distorted quote. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: What should an online program synopsis avoid?
options: Promising permissions or events not established
Guarantee all contracts are already cleared
Call broadcast-only music permission worldwide streaming rights
Remove crucial context from an interview silently
questions.rationale: Catalog descriptions must be accurate. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: Why prepare captions before final pilot delivery?
options: Accessibility is a defined program deliverable
Describe staged acts as documentary evidence
Treat each segment as having unlimited airtime
Guarantee all contracts are already cleared
questions.rationale: Subtitles should not be accidental last-minute work. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: What is appropriate if the music rights cover broadcast only?
options: Call broadcast-only music permission worldwide streaming rights
Remove crucial context from an interview silently
Describe staged acts as documentary evidence
Resolve separate online rights or revise the streaming version
questions.rationale: Broadcast clearance may not include online replay. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: What should a pilot segment rundown include?
options: Treat each segment as having unlimited airtime
Guarantee all contracts are already cleared
Durations, content and responsible people
Call broadcast-only music permission worldwide streaming rights
questions.rationale: Timing and ownership enable feasible production. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: Why should the social promotional clips be checked independently?
options: Remove crucial context from an interview silently
Short clips can strip critical context from longer material
Describe staged acts as documentary evidence
Treat each segment as having unlimited airtime
questions.rationale: Derivatives should still preserve honest meaning. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: The pilot segments last 8, 10, 6, 4 and 2 minutes. What is the total planned length?
options: 30 minutes
28 minutes
26 minutes
32 minutes
questions.rationale: 8+10+6+4+2=30. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.

questions.stem: A 30-minute draft runs to 32 minutes. By how much must its duration be reduced, absent slot changes?
options: 1 minute
4 minutes
8 minutes
2 minutes
questions.rationale: 32 minus 30 equals two minutes; edits must preserve meaning. Source: MAIC Media Studies - Entertainment and Broadcast Media, page 11.
